title: Flyto2 Core: http.paginate follows server-supplied next-page URLs (Link header / cursor) without SSRF revalidation
description:
Summary
http.paginate validates only the initial base_url, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 Link: rel="next" headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop without revalidating each follow-up URL. An attacker's first-page response can point next at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

Root Cause
src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495 validates base_url (first URL only). The pagination loop _paginate_link_header reads next_url via _parse_link_header (:203), sets url=next_url (:208), and calls session.request(method, url) (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

Impact
Readable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; int

title: django-docutils unsafe Docutils defaults allow local file disclosure, SSRF, and stored XSS

Summary

django-docutils before 0.30.0 rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. Public rendering paths, including publish_doctree, publish_html_from_source, publish_html_from_doctree, publish_parts_from_doctree, the {% rst %} template tag, the rst template filter, DocutilsTemplates, and DocutilsView, could process attacker-controlled RST with Docutils directives that read local files, fetch URL-backed content, or emit raw HTML.

The issue is fixed in 0.30.0 by disabling Docutils file insertion, raw directives, local docutils.conf processing, and unsafe URI schemes by default, and by sanitizing doctrees before HTML is emitted.

Details

title: NATS Server allows unauthenticated memory exhaustion through incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets
description:
Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients, including authentication and parsing of MQTT CONNECT packets.

Problem Description

An unauthenticated MQTT client could cause the server to retain large incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets before authentication completed.

The parser retained partial pre-authentication packet data while waiting for the advertised MQTT packet length to be completed. An attacker could therefore consume server memory until authentication timeouts closed the connections.

Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

title: NLTK: AllowlistUnpickler does not deny numpy submodule-local file-I/O sinks
description:
Summary

nltk.picklesec.allowlisted_pickle_load keyed its denylist of dangerous globals by export name, so numpy's file-I/O callables that live in submodules and are not re-exported under __module__ == "numpy" were never matched. Under the broad allowed_modules=("numpy", "scipy", "sklearn") allowance that TransitionParser.parse(depgraphs, modelFile) granted for model files, a crafted protocol 4 pickle could name numpy.lib._npyio_impl.recfromtxt (arbitrary file read, result returned to the caller of allowlisted_pickle_load) or numpy.lib.format.open_memmap (attacker-chosen file create), and the REDUCE opcode invoked them during the load.

Affected

nltk >= 3.10.0 and <= 3.10.3 (the allowlisting unpickler and the TransitionParser model path); numpy must be installed.

description:
Summary

StreamBackedCorpusView, a public API in nltk/corpus/reader/util.py, applies the pathsec sandbox to the file content it reads but not to the file metadata it probes in its constructor. When the view is created with a plain string fileid, __init__ calls os.stat(self._fileid).st_size with no pathsec validation, so an application that passes an attacker influenced path to the constructor discloses whether an arbitrary out of root file exists and, if it does, its exact byte size and modification time, even when nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE is True. This is the residual metadata channel left open by the fix for CVE-2026-63312 (GHSA-x5ph-mj9p-rfr8), which closed arbitrary content read on the same code path but did not bring the sibling os.stat under the sandbox.

title: NLTK: Untrusted search path in prover9/mace4 config allows local code execution via relative binary_location

Summary

(and Mace, which inherits it) accepts a relative binary_location and passes it as path_to_bin to find_binary, which disables the CWD-relative rejection guard. title: Guard Core: Quadratic ReDoS in built-in detection pattern freezes the event loop with a single request
description:
Summary

A polynomial (quadratic) regular-expression denial of service in guard-core's built-in penetration-detection patterns allows any unauthenticated remote client to freeze every endpoint of an application for seconds per request, using only the default configuration. title: k8s-mcp-server: Missing authentication on default SSE/HTTP transport allows unauthenticated Kubernetes tool execution
description:
Summary
When k8s-mcp-server runs in its default SSE transport mode, the MCP tools/call
endpoint is dispatched with no authentication, session token, or Origin check.
Any client that can reach the listening port can enumerate and invoke the
server's Kubernetes tools (including destructive/write tools) without credentials,
executing with the server's configured cluster privileges.

Affected
Commit be87a6dd72bb6ec1d4886b8548843b99a4638b12 (Merge PR #130)
MCP library: github.com/mark3labs/mcp-go v0.57.0
Default mode: sse (SERVER_MODE default), default port 8080, bind 0.0.0.0

Root cause (static trace: handleSSE -> handleMessage -> tools/call)
- main.go L129: server.NewSSEServer(s) is created with no auth option and no
 contextFunc; L130 sse.Start(":"+port) binds all interfaces

title: eml_parser: Algorithmic-complexity DoS (O(n^4) regex backtracking) in Received-header parsing
description:
Summary

eml_parser.routing.parserouting() dynamically builds a regex from up to four greedy .* groups (from (?P.*)by (?P.*)with (?P.*)for (?P.*)) terminated by an escaped literal of the date extracted from a normalized copy of the Received header. Because the date literal comes from the normalized text but is searched in the original line, a crafted header can make the trailing literal unmatchable; the search then fails at every start position only after exhaustively backtracking the four nested greedy groups — O(n^4) in header length. A single ~5.9 KB email pins one CPU core for ~12 seconds; doubling the input multiplies the cost ~25x, so a ~13 KB header takes minutes and a ~25 KB header effectively hangs the parse worker.

description:
Summary

shell/completion.zsh feeds every trigger-driven zsh completion through a FIFO at a predictable, PID-based path in shared /tmp (fzf-complete-fifo-$$), without checking the failure of rm -f/mkfifo. On a multi-user host, another local user can pre-create that path as a symlink to a victim-writable file (e.g. ~/.bashrc), causing the victim's own completion to overwrite it with the completion stream — with attacker-influenced content (e.g. via process names in ps output), escalating to code execution at the victim's next login. A pre-created plain FIFO instead leaks/blocks on the completion stream.

One unauthenticated GET request can poison the fallback shell cache entry that a family of routes shares.

Such a route is served from a shell that keeps its never-prerenderable params as placeholders, so every value of those params shares one cache entry. title: Todoist MCP Server: Browser DNS rebinding lets websites write and delete Todoist data through local MCP server
description:
The self-hosted todoist-mcp-http server accepts browser-origin MCP requests with attacker-controlled Host and Origin headers. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding to route its own origin to a victim's local 127.0.0.1 MCP server, then invoke Todoist MCP tools without a caller credential.

This affects github.com/Doist/todoist-mcp at commit d2903e0d945d2a559d71c091337ad6380511e62f, package version 10.3.1, when the optional Streamable HTTP server is running. The stdio entrypoint is not browser-reachable. The vulnerable browser-reachable component is todoist-mcp-http.

The documented HTTP server mode runs all MCP tools with the operator's TODOIST_API_KEY and binds to loopback by default:

TODOIST_API_KEY=your-key npx -p @doist/todoist-mcp todoist-mcp-http

title: keystore-go: Keystore integrity and password verification bypass via stripped trailing digest in Decode()
description:
Summary
keystore.Decode() fails to check the error returned when reading the trailing SHA-1 integrity digest of a JKS keystore. If an attacker removes the final 20 bytes from a .jks file, the digest read returns an empty slice and the byte-comparison loop never executes, so Decode() returns the parsed keystore with err == nil. This defeats both tamper detection and — for certificate-only truststores — the password check itself, allowing an attacker with write access to a keystore file (but without knowledge of the keystore password) to silently inject or replace trusted CA certificates.

Details
Affected versions: github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go ≤ v2.1.0+incompatible (the final release on this module path). v3 and v4 releases are not impacted.

title: OliveTin: Second-Order OS Command Injection via shellAfterCompleted
description:
Summary

OliveTin's shellAfterCompleted post-execution hook injects unsanitized variables — including arbitrary command output (output), the authenticated username (ot_username), and the exit code (exitCode) — directly into a shell command template processed by sh -c. Unlike the main action's argument handling, no checkShellArgumentSafety validation is applied to these variables. An attacker who can influence the output of a command (e.g., via user-supplied arguments that reflect in stdout, or through trusted-header username spoofing) can inject arbitrary OS commands into the post-execution shell.

title: mail-parser: Uncaught OverflowError / OSError on an out-of-range Received date
description:
Impact

A Received header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offset
large enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that is
outside the MailParser* hierarchy. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptions
does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue
as GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf (https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf),
which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes(), parse_from_file(),
parse_from_file_obj() and the mail-parser CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and
a single line is enough,

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

When a page, plugin or route middleware throws an error that is not an HTTP error, Nuxt wraps it with createError before rendering the error page. title: Nuxt payload URL generation has quadratic cost for repeated slashes in the request path
description:
Summary

Nuxt strips trailing slashes from the request path with a regular expression whose cost grows quadratically with the length of a run of consecutive slashes. A single unauthenticated request with a long run of slashes can occupy the server's event loop for a noticeable time, delaying every other request handled by the same process.

Impact

When a page is rendered with payload extraction (any route covered by an isr, swr or cache route rule), Nuxt builds the _payload.json URL from the raw request path. A path such as /blog/a followed by 16,000 slashes and x, which fits within Node's default header size limit, takes roughly 0.1 to 0.4 seconds of synchronous CPU time per request, depending on hardware. Workaround

Use at most one * in a domain mask.

title: AIOHTTP: Base64 multipart parts bypass client_max_size
description:
Summary

When reading a multipart part with Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, BodyPartReader.read_chunk() kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short Content-Length, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.

Impact

An attacker could bypass client_max_size to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fdd

title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket max_msg_size bypass via integer overflow
description:
Summary

The max_msg_size check in the WebSocket reader added the declared frame length to the size of the partial message already buffered. In the C extension this addition is 64-bit arithmetic, so a declared length close to 2**63 overflowed and the check passed.

Impact

An attacker could bypass max_msg_size and cause unbounded memory use by streaming an oversized WebSocket message after a small non-final fragment.

Workaround

If unable to upgrade, the Python reader is unaffected and can be used with AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8cfbe9abe5e11b84006a10f9bdf82bf607671dab

description:

Impact

An attacker could cause unbounded memory use by streaming data behind an upgrade request to any handler that does not immediately accept or reject the upgrade.

title: AIOHTTP: Pure-Python parser request replay and buffer growth behind a declined upgrade
description:
Summary

When the pipelined request queue was full, the pure-Python parser stored the unparsed remainder internally and also returned it to the caller. After a handler declined an upgrade request, the buffered data was re-fed, so the buffer grew with each handled request and already-handled requests were dispatched to the application again.

Impact

If users are using the Python parser (AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS, or not a standard wheel installed), an attacker could cause excessive memory use and cause pipelined requests to be processed more than once.

Workaround

Switch to the default C parser.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47babd8c23ca79e2bae6cc8dcb5752b61e369fc7

title: AIOHTTP: Concatenated compressed streams cause excessive CPU use
description:
Summary

When decompressing a payload made up of many concatenated compressed members (gzip, deflate or zstd), each member was decoded by passing the entire remaining input to a new decompressor, resulting in quadratic CPU time. Empty members produce no output, so client_max_size and output backpressure did not limit the work.

Impact

An attacker could block the event loop of a server with a specially crafted compressed request body or WebSocket message. A malicious server could do the same to a client.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/d925a80539ffd227da1d93ab4a5bff123cc777db

title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket receive queue limits bypassed by small or compressed messages
description:
Summary

The WebSocket reader continued parsing frames already received after the receive queue had paused the transport, and empty messages were not counted towards the queue size. With permessage-deflate, a single read of compressed frames could add many megabytes of decompressed messages to the queue.

Impact

An attacker could cause excessive memory use in a WebSocket server, or a malicious server against a client, by sending many small or compressed messages faster than the application consumes them.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/0ae507423f681161efa77d20052b4054397c7fb6

title: NLTK: Symlink escape in chat80.sql_query bypasses the pathsec data-root sandbox to read out-of-root SQLite databases
description:
Summary

nltk.sem.chat80.sql_query() opens a SQLite database by handing the result of nltk.data.find(dbname) straight to sqlite3.connect() without the path-containment check that the NLTK data sandbox (nltk.pathsec) is meant to enforce. nltk.data.find() applies only lexical checks to the resource name and returns a FileSystemPathPointer whose path is normalized with os.path.abspath but never resolved for symlinks. As a result, an in-root symbolic link that points at a SQLite file outside every registered NLTK data root is followed by SQLite, and the caller receives query results from the out-of-sandbox database.
